title: Enacted Swedish wage-earner funds, 1984–1991
summary: Separates the enacted five-board pension-fund compromise from the earlier open-ended Meidner proposal and examines its ownership, delegation, and abolition rules.

sources.title: Proposition 1983/84:50 om löntagarfonder
sources.authorityNote: The government proposition specifies the enacted boards, funding, appointment, ownership, voting, delegation, and evaluation rules.

sources.title: Proposition 1991/92:36 om avveckling av löntagarfonderna
sources.authorityNote: The government proposition documents the abolition proposal and transfer to a liquidation board.

sources.title: From Marxist Venture to Venture Capitalists: The Swedish Wage-Earner Funds and the Market Turn, 1983–1994
sources.authorityNote: An open-access business-history study of the funds’ rules, board operation, portfolio, performance, and political dismantling.

claims.text: The enacted arrangement created five independent government-appointed boards within the public pension system, funded through specified payroll and profit levies and constrained by funding and company-vote caps.
limitations: Formal statutory rules do not by themselves establish how authority operated in practice.

claims.text: Local unions could request delegation of half the voting rights attached to a board’s shares in their company.
limitations: The existence of a delegation rule does not show how frequently or effectively it was used.

claims.text: At the end of 1991 the funds held approximately 2.6 percent of stock-exchange value and had generally come to operate as investment companies rather than controlling owners.
limitations: Aggregate ownership share does not capture every firm-level influence or non-listed investment.

claims.text: The five boards were abolished at the end of 1991 and their assets transferred to a liquidation board.
limitations: The abolition date does not by itself identify the relative causal weight of ideology, electoral change, performance, or economic conditions.

conflictingEvidence.summary: The enacted design can be interpreted either as a politically diluted ownership-transfer mechanism or as a deliberate pluralist limit on delegated fund power. Statutory caps establish the design but do not resolve which normative interpretation should dominate.

limitations: The enacted compromise must not be conflated with the 1975 Meidner proposal.
The case is evidence about one contested Swedish episode, not social democracy generally.

relationships.reason: The enacted compromise pursued contested goals inside Swedish social-democratic politics without defining the whole tradition.
The design explicitly altered collective capital claims while imposing ownership and voting caps.
Appointment, delegation, voting caps, audits, and legislative abolition expose multiple accountability channels.
Income, ownership, control, and pension returns must be evaluated separately.
The appointed boards and delegated votes require explicit assessment of representation and contestability.

proposedRelationships.reason: The board, funding, investment, and voting rules form a distinct institutional mechanism.

duplicateCandidates.reason: The tradition revision proposes this same companion case relationship; this file supplies the independently reviewable case entity.

content.name: Enacted Swedish wage-earner funds
content.scope: Covers the five enacted AP-system fund boards from their establishment through abolition; excludes treating the more radical 1975 proposal as enacted policy.
content.selectionRationale: Tests how formal ownership and delegation limits shaped distribution, control, accountability, and political durability.
conditions: Polarized conflict between organized labor and business
Government appointment and parliamentary authority over the fund rules
outcomes: Investor behavior closer to conventional investment companies than controlling owners
Abolition following the 1991 change of government
rivalExplanations: Design dilution, market conditions, business opposition, board experience, and partisan turnover may each explain different outcomes
transferLimitations: Swedish pension institutions and organized-interest structures were case-specific
Short duration and political contestation constrain performance inference
